• Disabled children are those who have physical, sensory, intellectual, or developmental impairments that can affect their ability to participate in typical educational and social activities.
 
• They may require special education services, assistive technologies, and tailored healthcare interventions to enhance their quality of life.
 
• Organizations and individuals working for disabled children often focus on providing inclusive education, early intervention programs, and vocational training.
 
• Support systems for disabled children aim to empower them to achieve their full potential and lead independent lives.
 
 
 
• **Destitute Children**
 
 
• Destitute children are those who lack basic necessities such as food, shelter, and parental care due to extreme poverty, abandonment, or loss of parents.
 
• They are highly vulnerable and often require immediate intervention to ensure their safety and well-being.
 
• Programs for destitute children typically include provision of shelter homes, nutritional support, educational opportunities, and psychological counseling.
 
• Efforts are made to rehabilitate these children by reuniting them with family members if possible or by providing long-term care solutions such as adoption or foster care.

• Rehabilitation services for children with disabilities and those in destitute situations include medical, psychological, social, and educational interventions aimed at improving their overall functioning.
 
• These services help children develop essential life skills, improve mobility, and enhance their ability to communicate and interact with others.
 
• Rehabilitation may involve physical therapy, speech therapy, occupational therapy, and counseling.
 
• The goal is to enable these children to lead fulfilling lives and integrate into their communities.

• It promotes equality and participation by ensuring that every child has access to quality education.
 
• Inclusive education involves adapting teaching methods, curricula, and learning environments to meet the diverse needs of all students.

questions.question: Lasers have a wide range of applications across various fields. The acronym 'LASER' stands for _____.

options.text: Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation
Light Amplification by Spontaneous Emission of Radiation
Laser Application in Scientific and Experimental Research

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The acronym LASER stands for **Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation**, which highlights the fundamental process behind laser operation.
 
• Lasers emit light through a process of **optical amplification** based on the stimulated emission of electromagnetic radiation.
 
• This technology has a wide range of applications, including **medicine, communication, manufacturing, defense, and scientific research**.
 
• The concept of stimulated emission was initially proposed by **Albert Einstein in 1917**, forming the theoretical basis for laser technology.
 
• The first operational laser was developed by **Theodore Maiman in 1960**, using a synthetic ruby crystal as the medium.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Stimulated Emission**

 
 
• Stimulated emission occurs when an incoming photon of a specific energy causes an excited electron to drop to a lower energy level, emitting a photon of the same energy, phase, and direction.
 
• This principle is the cornerstone of laser operation, ensuring coherent light emission.
 
 
 
• **Types of Lasers**
 
 
• Lasers are classified based on the medium used, such as solid-state lasers (e.g., ruby lasers), gas lasers (e.g., CO₂ lasers), semiconductor lasers, and dye lasers.
 
• Each type of laser is suited for specific applications, such as industrial cutting (CO₂ lasers) or medical procedures (Nd:YAG lasers).
 
 
 
• **Applications of Lasers**
 
 
• In medicine, lasers are used for surgeries, skin treatments, and eye corrections (e.g., LASIK).
 
• In communication, laser technology is integral to optical fiber networks for high-speed data transmission.
 
• In manufacturing, lasers are employed for cutting, welding, and engraving materials with precision.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of Laser Light**
 
 
• Laser light is **monochromatic**, meaning it consists of a single wavelength.
 
• It is highly **coherent**, ensuring the light waves are in phase and travel in the same direction.
 
• Laser light is also **directional**, producing a narrow and focused beam.

• Examples include the **tabla, drum, and xylophone**.
 
• They are primarily used to maintain rhythm and are not melodic like the harmonium.
 
• Percussion instruments do not utilize air or wind to produce sound, which is a key characteristic of the harmonium.

questions.question: Which Constitutional amendment led to the introduction of the Goods and Services Tax (GST) in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**101st Amendment**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The 101st Constitutional Amendment Act was passed by the Parliament of India in August 2016.
 
• This amendment led to the introduction of the Goods and Services Tax (GST), which came into effect from 1st July 2017.
 
• GST replaced multiple indirect taxes like VAT, service tax, excise duty, etc., with a single tax regime.
 
• The amendment aimed to streamline the tax structure and enhance the efficiency of the tax system in India.
 
• The GST Council was established under this amendment to make recommendations on various GST-related issues.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Goods and Services Tax (GST)**

 
 
• GST is a comprehensive, multi-stage, destination-based tax that is levied on every value addition.
 
• It is divided into Central GST (CGST), State GST (SGST), Integrated GST (IGST), and Union Territory GST (UTGST).
 
• GST has subsumed numerous indirect taxes such as excise duty, VAT, service tax, and more.
 
• It simplifies the taxation system and reduces the cascading effect of taxes by allowing seamless input tax credit.
 
• The GST regime aims to create a unified market and promote economic growth by reducing tax evasion and enhancing transparency.
 
 
 
• **GST Council**
 
 
• The GST Council is a constitutional body established under Article 279A.
 
• It comprises the Union Finance Minister, the Union Minister of State for Finance, and the Finance Ministers of all states.
 
• The council is responsible for making recommendations on aspects like tax rates, exemptions, thresholds, and other matters related to GST.
 
• Decisions in the GST Council are made by a majority of not less than three-fourths of the weighted votes of the members present.
 
 
 
• **Input Tax Credit (ITC)**
 
 
• ITC allows businesses to claim the tax paid on purchase of goods and services used for business purposes.
 
• It helps in reducing the overall tax liability and ensures that tax is paid only on the value addition.
 
• ITC is available for both goods and services under the GST regime.
 
 
 
• **GST Rates**
 
 
• GST has multiple rates ranging from 0%, 5%, 12%, 18%, to 28%, based on the type of goods and services.
 
• Luxury items and sin goods attract higher tax rates, whereas essential goods and services are taxed at lower rates.

questions.question: At the time of Independence, what was the major characteristic of India's economy?

• Agriculture contributed to **more than 50% of the GDP** during this period.
 
• Approximately **70-75% of the Indian workforce** was employed in the agriculture sector.
 
• Industrial and urban development was minimal, with **limited infrastructure** and industrial output.

• **Land Reforms**

 
 
• Post-Independence, India implemented various land reforms to redistribute land to the landless and marginal farmers.
 
• Key measures included the abolition of the zamindari system, tenancy reforms, and ceiling on landholdings.
 
 
 
• **Green Revolution**
 
 
• Introduced in the 1960s, the Green Revolution aimed to increase agricultural productivity through high-yielding variety (HYV) seeds, fertilizers, and irrigation.
 
• It significantly boosted food grain production, especially in states like Punjab, Haryana, and Uttar Pradesh.
 
 
 
• **Five-Year Plans**
 
 
• The Government of India adopted a series of Five-Year Plans to strategize and implement economic development goals.
 
• The First Five-Year Plan (1951-1956) focused heavily on agricultural development and land reforms.

• India's rural economy was characterized by small and fragmented landholdings, subsistence farming, and low productivity.
 
• Rural infrastructure, including roads, electricity, and irrigation, was underdeveloped.

questions.question: Social or Collective Ownership, Central Planning Authority and Social Welfare are the features of which type of economy?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Socialism**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Socialism** is an economic system where **social or collective ownership** of resources and production is emphasized.
 
• It is characterized by the presence of a **Central Planning Authority** that regulates and plans the allocation of resources to achieve equitable outcomes.
 
• The primary goal of socialism is to ensure **social welfare**, focusing on reducing inequalities and providing basic needs like healthcare, education, and housing to all citizens.
 
• Under socialism, the government or collective entities own and control major industries and services, such as transportation, energy, and healthcare, to prevent exploitation and ensure fair distribution.
 
• Countries like **China, Cuba, and Vietnam** have implemented socialist principles to varying degrees, often combining them with other economic systems.
 
• Socialism contrasts with capitalism, where private ownership and profit-maximization are prioritized.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Capitalism**__

 __
 
• **Capitalism** is an economic system where production and resources are owned privately, and decisions regarding production and pricing are determined by market forces.
 
• It promotes **individual profit** and competitive markets, emphasizing minimal government intervention.
 
• Countries like **United States, Japan, and Germany** primarily follow capitalist systems.
 
• While it fosters innovation and economic growth, capitalism can lead to significant income inequality.
 
 
 
• **Imperialism**__
 __
 
• **Imperialism** refers to the policy of extending a nation's power and influence through colonization, military force, or other means.
 
• Historically, countries such as **Britain, France, and Spain** engaged in imperialism during the colonial era.
 
• It often led to exploitation of resources and suppression of local cultures in colonized regions.
 
 
 
• **Communism**__
 
 
• **Communism** is a political and economic ideology advocating for a classless society where all property is publicly owned.
 
• It aims to eliminate private ownership and ensure equal distribution of wealth.
 
• Countries like **Cuba and North Korea** have adopted communist frameworks, focusing on centralized control of all economic and social activities.
 
• While communism seeks equality, its implementation has often faced challenges such as lack of incentives and political authoritarianism.

questions.question: Who among the following thinkers introduced the Human Development Index for the first time in 1990?

• **Mahbub-ul-Haq**, a Pakistani economist, introduced the **Human Development Index (HDI)** in 1990.
 
• HDI was developed as part of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)’s **Human Development Report** under his leadership.
 
• The HDI measures a country’s development using three key dimensions: **health (life expectancy), education, and standard of living (GNI per capita).**
 
• The HDI aimed to shift the focus from economic growth alone to a more comprehensive understanding of human development.
 
• Mahbub-ul-Haq collaborated with Indian economist **Amartya Sen** in conceptualizing and refining the HDI framework.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Human Development Index (HDI):**

 
 
• Introduced in the first **UNDP Human Development Report (1990)**.
 
• It combines indicators of life expectancy, education (mean years of schooling and expected years of schooling), and income (GNI per capita) into a single composite index.
 
• HDI values range from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating better development outcomes.
 
 
 
• **Mahbub-ul-Haq’s Contributions:**
 
 
• He emphasized the importance of human welfare and development over mere economic indicators like GDP.
 
• He played a key role in advocating for poverty reduction and equitable development policies globally.
 
 
 
• **Human Development Report:**
 
 
• Published annually by the UNDP, it ranks countries based on their HDI scores.
 
• The report provides insights into global developmental challenges and policy recommendations.
 
 
 
• **Amartya Sen:**
 
 
• An Indian economist and Nobel laureate who collaborated with Mahbub-ul-Haq on HDI development.
 
• Sen’s work on human capability and welfare economics greatly influenced the HDI framework.

questions.question: Which are the three main sector classifications of the Indian economy?

• **Secondary Sector:** This sector includes industries that process raw materials obtained from the primary sector into finished goods, such as manufacturing and construction.
 
• **Tertiary Sector:** This sector provides services to businesses and individuals, such as trade, transport, banking, healthcare, and education.
 
• The classification helps in understanding the economic structure and contribution of each sector to India's GDP and employment.

• **Secondary Sector Insights:**
 
 
• Known as the **industrial sector**, it contributes significantly to the GDP through manufacturing and infrastructure development.
 
• It includes industries like textiles, automobile, and steel production, which are key to India's industrial growth.
 
 
 
• **Tertiary Sector Insights:**
 
 
• The tertiary sector, or the **service sector**, is the largest contributor to India's GDP.

• Major cotton-growing regions in Gujarat include **Saurashtra, Kutch, and parts of North Gujarat**.

__
 
• During the **colonial period**, India's foreign trade was heavily influenced and controlled by **British policies**. The British used India as a source of raw materials and as a market for their finished goods.
 
• India's trade was largely focused on exporting raw materials like **cotton, jute, and indigo**, while importing manufactured goods from Britain, such as **textiles, machinery, and tools**.
 
• The colonial government implemented policies that restricted India's trade relations with other countries like **Sri Lanka, China, and Iran**, ensuring that most trade benefited Britain.
 
• The **drain of wealth theory**, proposed by Indian nationalists like **Dadabhai Naoroji**, explained how India's resources were extracted and profits were sent to Britain, leaving India impoverished.
 
• This trade pattern led to the decline of indigenous industries, such as **handloom weaving**, as cheaper British goods flooded the Indian market.
 
• India's dependence on Britain for trade and economic policies left its economy vulnerable to exploitation and limited the scope for diversification or economic independence.
 
• Colonial trade policies were designed to serve the economic interests of the **British Empire**, rather than the development of India's economy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **India's foreign trade greatly benefited the economy and eliminated shortages of essential goods**__

 __
 
• This statement is incorrect because India's foreign trade during the colonial period did not benefit the economy but rather led to **economic exploitation**.
 
• The trade policies were designed to benefit Britain, and shortages of essential goods often persisted due to the prioritization of exports over local consumption.
 
 
 
• **India imported raw materials and exported finished goods**__
 __
 
• This option is incorrect as the opposite was true. India exported **raw materials** like cotton and jute and imported **manufactured goods** from Britain.
 
• The export of raw materials and the import of finished goods caused the decline of **local industries**.
 
 
 
• **India primarily traded with European nations other than Britain**__
 
 
• This option is incorrect as India's trade during the colonial period was overwhelmingly dominated by Britain, with minimal trade relationships with other European nations.
 
• Trade with other nations like **China and Sri Lanka** was limited and often controlled by British policies.

questions.question: What is globalisation?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Integration of economies worldwide**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Globalisation** refers to the process of increasing **interconnectedness and integration** among countries, primarily in terms of their **economies, cultures, and political systems**.
 
• It involves the **free flow of goods, services, capital, technology, and information** across international borders.
 
• Globalisation has been facilitated by advancements in **technology**, such as the internet and communication systems, and the reduction of **trade barriers** like tariffs and quotas.
 
• It enables countries to participate in the **global market**, leading to the development of international trade networks and collaborative partnerships.
 
• Examples include the establishment of **multinational corporations**, the rise of global supply chains, and the widespread adoption of international trade agreements.
 
• Globalisation promotes **economic growth**, increases **employment opportunities**, and fosters **cultural exchange**, but it also raises concerns about **inequality**, **environmental degradation**, and **loss of local identity**.
 
• Key organisations like the **World Trade Organization (WTO)**, **International Monetary Fund (IMF)**, and **World Bank** play a significant role in managing and promoting globalisation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **A political alliance between countries**__

 __
 
• A political alliance generally refers to a formal agreement between countries to work together on specific issues, such as defense or diplomacy.
 
• Examples include organisations like **NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organization)** or the **European Union (EU)**, which focus on political, economic, and military cooperation.
 
• While alliances play a role in international relations, they are distinct from the broader economic and cultural integration involved in globalisation.
 
 
 
• **Decline in international trade**__
 __
 
• A decline in international trade refers to reduced trade activity between nations, often caused by factors like **economic downturns, protectionist policies, or geopolitical tensions**.
 
• This is the opposite of globalisation, which aims to increase international trade and economic connectivity.
 
 
 
• **An increase in cultural isolation**__
 
 
• Cultural isolation refers to the separation of cultures, where societies avoid influence or interaction with others.
 
• Globalisation, on the other hand, fosters **cultural exchange** and interaction through mediums like **media, travel, and trade**.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the concept of offshoring?

options.text: Transferring certain company tasks or services to a foreign country to lower expenses
Hiring temporary workers for short-term projects
Relocating business operations to another area within the same country
Decreasing wages within the company to boost profits

questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Transferring certain company tasks or services to a foreign country to lower expenses**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Offshoring** refers to the practice of relocating specific company operations, tasks, or services to a **foreign country** to reduce costs, such as labor or production expenses.
 
• This is often done to leverage **lower wages**, **tax benefits**, or **less expensive operational costs** in the target country.
 
• Key industries that utilize offshoring include **information technology**, **manufacturing**, **customer service**, and **back-office operations**.
 
• Countries like **India**, **China**, and the **Philippines** are popular offshoring destinations due to their **skilled workforce** and **cost advantages**.
 
• Offshoring should not be confused with **outsourcing**, although the two concepts are often interrelated. Outsourcing refers to hiring a third-party organization to perform tasks, while offshoring specifically refers to moving tasks to a foreign location.
 
• Benefits of offshoring include **cost reduction**, **24/7 operations** (due to time zone differences), and access to a **larger talent pool**.
 
• Challenges of offshoring may include issues related to **language barriers**, **cultural differences**, and **geopolitical risks**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Hiring temporary workers for short-term projects**__

 __
 
• This refers to the practice of hiring **contract workers** or **freelancers** for specific projects or tasks.
 
• It is different from offshoring as it does not necessarily involve **relocating tasks to another country**.
 
• Examples include hiring **freelancers** for content writing, graphic design, or software development.
 
 
 
• **Relocating business operations to another area within the same country**__
 __
 
• This is known as **onshoring** or **domestic relocation**.
 
• It involves moving operations from one region of a country to another, often to benefit from **lower domestic costs** or access to specific resources.
 
• For example, a company in the **United States** might relocate its operations from a high-cost urban area to a rural region.
 
 
 
• **Decreasing wages within the company to boost profits**__
 
 
• This strategy is not related to offshoring. It refers to **internal cost-cutting measures** such as reducing employee salaries to improve profit margins.
 
• Such practices can have negative effects, including **reduced employee morale** and **higher turnover rates**.

questions.question: Which fiscal condition related to India's trade balance did the Economic Survey 2024 report for FY24?

options.text: Increased trade deficit compared to FY23

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Narrowed trade deficit**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Economic Survey 2024 reported that India's trade deficit **narrowed in FY24** compared to previous fiscal years, reflecting an improvement in the country's external trade balance.
 
• This narrowing was attributed to factors such as **increased exports of services** and a reduction in the import bill for energy commodities like crude oil.
 
• India's merchandise exports saw a **moderate growth**, while imports declined slightly due to **lower global commodity prices**.
 
• The survey highlighted the resilience of India's economy amidst global challenges, with a **focus on boosting exports** and reducing dependency on imports.
 
• Strong performance in the IT and services sectors played a critical role in offsetting the merchandise trade deficit.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Trade Deficit:** A trade deficit occurs when a country's imports exceed its exports, leading to a negative balance of trade.
 
• **Service Exports:** India's IT and financial services sectors contribute significantly to overall exports, helping reduce the trade deficit.
 
• **Global Commodity Prices:** Fluctuations in prices of commodities like crude oil, natural gas, and metals directly impact India's import bill.
 
• **Current Account Deficit (CAD):** The trade deficit is a major component of the current account. A narrowed trade deficit helps in reducing the CAD, which is crucial for economic stability.
 
• **Government Initiatives:** Programs like the Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme aim to boost manufacturing and reduce import dependency, thereby improving the trade balance.
